THE GATEKEEPERS 
CORRUPTION RISKS WITH MINISTERIAL ADVISORS
What needs to change
The governance and accountability of ministerial staff ought to be strengthened to 
better reflect the nature of the roles and the risks of corruption.  It is important, too, that 
ministerial staff have an awareness of their vulnerability to corruption and can recognise 
attempts at being groomed or influenced.  
The following recommendations have been put to the Premier:
RECOMMENDATION 1
Review existing recruitment processes for the appointment of ministerial staff to 
ensure current practices align with public sector guidelines.29 In particular, ensure 
that prospective ministerial staff are subject to pre-employment screening. 
RECOMMENDATION 2
Introduce the requirement that all ministerial staff obtain and maintain security 
clearance to at least Negative Vetting Level 1. 
RECOMMENDATION 3
Review existing induction processes for ministerial staff and ensure they include 
education and training on the following:
	
⊲
the Code of Ethics for the South Australian public sector
	
⊲
obligations to report conflicts of interests and pecuniary interests
	
⊲
corruption risks associated with the role (including recognising corruption 
vulnerabilities and grooming)
RECOMMENDATION 4
Introduce compulsory training for ministerial advisors every 2 years, including in 
the Code of Ethics, and obligations to report conflicts of interests and pecuniary 
interests.

RECOMMENDATION 5
Introduce a requirement that all chiefs of staff provide the Commissioner for Public 
Sector Employment with an annual declaration that ministerial staff have met their 
obligations in respect of conflicts of interests and pecuniary interest declarations, and 
that induction programs and compulsory training referred to in Recommendation 4 
are up to date.
RECOMMENDATION 6
Consider developing a Ministerial Staff Code of Conduct that deals with matters 
including soliciting or accepting bribes and attempting to influence decisions for 
personal gain or to favour a third party.  
Conclusion
A great deal of trust is placed in ministerial advisors. Along with that comes risk.
It is important for an assessment to be made of an individual’s vulnerability to engage in 
corrupt conduct both before they are appointed and during their tenure. The Government 
has a responsibility to properly induct ministerial staff so that obligations and expectations 
are adequately communicated. It must also ensure that robust and appropriate 
accountability mechanisms are in place to monitor both the ongoing risks and the 
effectiveness of the controls to manage those risks.
Government ministers should ask themselves: How well do I know my advisors?
